subtitles.text: My girlfriend has a slightly unusual
hobby. She likes tracking ships. And no,
I don't mean that she sits at the harbor
all day with a pair of binoculars. She
actually likes opening one of these
websites where you can see all the ships
around the world and then checking where
they're going, what kind of ship it is,
and where it came from. So, because I
love her and because apparently I can't
just buy normal gifts, I thought it
would be a nice idea to build her a
device that can do exactly that. And
this is what I ended up with. It's an
e-ink ship tracker that can show the
ships in a certain area, lets you browse
through them, and even follow a specific
ship. And to explain how this thing
works, let's start with the hardware.
At the heart of the tracker is a
Raspberry Pi Zero W. And the nerds among
you probably already know that this
isn't exactly the newest Raspberry Pi
anymore. My original idea was actually
to use a Pi Zero 2 W, but Raspberry Pis
have become surprisingly expensive.
>> [music] >> For the display, I chose this 7.5-in
Waveshare e-ink display. It can display
multiple shades of gray. It looks really
nice. And compared to some other e-ink
displays, the refresh rate is actually
pretty decent.
But before I could really start putting
any of this together, I had to solve
what was probably the biggest problem of
the entire project. Where do I actually
get the ship data?
There are obviously plenty of websites
and apps where you can track almost
every ship in the world, but I can't
simply take their data and use it for my
own device. Some of them don't offer a
suitable API and simply scraping their
websites wasn't really an option either.
For a while, I wasn't even sure if this
project was going to work at all, until
I discovered something I really didn't
expect.
Finland. Finland makes a huge amount of
its transportation data publicly available, including AIS data for ships,
which was basically exactly what I
needed. So, genuinely big shout out to
Finland because without them, this project probably wouldn't exist. Finland
also isn't the only place where
something like this might be possible.
While researching this, Norway and Singapore also stood out to me because
they seem to be relatively open with at
least some of their maritime data.
Now that I finally had the data, I could
start connecting the display to the
Raspberry Pi and think about what the
actual interface should look like. But
while doing that, I realized I had
forgotten something fairly important.
How am I actually going to control this
thing? I didn't really want to use a
touchscreen because I wanted the device
to stay as simple as possible, and
adding a whole row of buttons didn't
really fit the design either. My
solution was to use two rotary encoders.
Both of them can obviously rotate in
either direction, but they also have a
button built into them.
>> [bell] >> Connecting everything to the Raspberry
Pi wasn't particularly difficult,
although I was slightly annoyed to
discover that the GPIO pins aren't
actually labeled [music] on the board.
The last thing missing on the hardware
side was power. The Pi Zero W is pretty
old at this point, which means it still
uses micro USB, and I really didn't want
to build a new device in 2026 that still
has a micro USB port. So, I added a
small USB-C breakout board and soldered
it directly to the power input of the
Raspberry Pi. It's a very small
addition, but now the whole device can
simply be powered over USB-C. With the
hardware basically working, I could finally start programming everything.
And And is where my original idea for
the interface started to fall apart a
little bit. Originally, I didn't just
want to show the name, position, and
information of a ship. I also wanted to
display an actual picture of it. And
technically, it actually did. The problem was the refresh time. The
display can do relatively fast partial
refreshes when I'm only changing simple
black and white elements, but I couldn't
get partial grayscale refreshes to work.
So, I decided to take a step back and as
much as it hurt, get rid of the ship
photos. Instead, I added a QR code to
the interface. On the main screen, you
see a section of the Gulf of Finland
where there's usually quite a lot
happening with cargo ships, tankers,
ferries, and all sorts of other vessels
moving through the area. From there, you
can switch between three different views. There's a recommended section
where the tracker picks particularly large or interesting ships. There's a
view where you can browse through all
the ships in the area, and then there's
a favorite section. If you find a ship
that you want to follow, you simply
press the encoder and it gets added as
your favorite. After you haven't touched
the device for a few minutes, it
automatically switches into what I call
sleep mode. The interface becomes much
cleaner, most of the menus disappear,
and the tracker continues following your
selected ship. With the second rotary
encoder, you can switch between the
different information available for each ship, and that's basically all I wanted
the interface to do. No complicated
menus or endless settings. Just two
knobs and a screen. Hopefully, that's
enough to keep my girlfriend entertained. Another nice side effect of
this relatively simple interface is that
the entire device doesn't use very much
power. The Raspberry Pi Zero W is
already quite efficient, and the e-paper
display basically only consumes power when something on the screen actually
changes. But before I could give this
thing to my girlfriend, there was still
one fairly obvious problem. It needed a
case.
I designed the whole thing in Shapr3D
and had to print one or two prototypes
until all the measurements finally worked. I designed a recessed area in
the front of the enclosure where the
display can sit and behind it there's a
separate back plate which also holds the
Raspberry Pi. The back plate is attached
with four screws, but I designed the
spacing so that even when everything is
tightened down, it can't actually press
directly against the display. To keep
the display from moving around, I added
some foam mounting tape. The foam
compresses slightly, so it gently holds
the display in position without putting
too much pressure on it.
>> [music] >> Once everything is connected, all that's
really missing is the bottom plate. And
suddenly, this mess of wires, a
Raspberry Pi, and an e-ink display
actually starts to look like a real
product. For the enclosure, I used my
usual matte muted white Pancroma PLA.
And while designing those parts, I also
got to try a new Shaper 3D feature for
the first time. Instead of exporting the
model, saving the file, and then
importing it into the slicer separately,
I could send the project directly from
Shaper 3D into PrusaSlicer, which sounds
like a very small thing, but when you're
constantly changing dimensions and printing new prototypes, removing that
extra step is actually really convenient. With the final knobs
installed, the ship tracker was finally
finished. But of course, there's still
one pretty important question. I built
this whole thing for my girlfriend. So,
what does she think?
>> [gasps] >> Luckily, she actually really likes it.
And honestly, it's pretty nice to
finally spend way too much time on a
project that isn't just for me. So, I
think this one was worth it. If you like
the project and want to build your own
ship tracker, I'll upload all the files
and a complete build guide to my Kofi.
And as always, you'll find links to all
the components, materials, and software I used down in the description. I'm
already looking forward to the next
project, and I hope I'll see you there.
Until then, ciao.
